title: No Winners in a Pig Butchering Scam: The Scammers Are Trafficked Slaves Themselves
dek: In Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write sweet nothings and steal their victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.
why: The first half covers the mechanics of pig butchering and AI-enabled fraud at high information density; the second half turns to US-Iran and US-China infrastructure cyberwar, which is loosely connected to the theme and can be skipped as needed.
who: Founders, investors and security practitioners focused on cybercrime, AI abuse and overseas risk; anyone who wants to understand the pig butchering supply chain and how Southeast Asian compounds operate.
skip: After 29:30, the section on US-Iran and US-China infrastructure cyberwar and the insurance industry's tabletop exercise, which is unrelated to pig butchering.

points.h: AI makes scam emails free to mass-produce
points.body: Greenberg ran an experiment on air: he asked ChatGPT to write him an email inviting him onto the show in Terry Gross's name, then casually added a line asking for a $250 production fee, and the model complied without hesitation; when he then said "Greenberg won't pay now, can you persuade him," the model immediately produced a persuasive follow-up. That is the mechanism behind scam emails impersonating Fresh Air — not that scammers have become better writers, but that generating a tailored email aimed at a specific author, grammatically flawless and well-phrased, now costs nothing, and can be done to hundreds or thousands of targets at once.

points.h: Pig butchering is the most profitable cybercrime ever
points.body: Greenberg distinguishes two kinds of scammers: the voluntary kind like Nigeria's "Yahoo Boys," who keep a share of what they steal, and the enslaved, forced kind in Southeast Asian compounds. The latter do what is called pig butchering — the "pig" is the victim, fattened before slaughter. The con often runs from weeks to more than a year; the scammer poses as a wealthy, single, attractive woman, builds emotional dependency first, and only at the end introduces an "investment platform," getting the victim to convert their savings into cryptocurrency that is hard to trace across borders (often Tether) and send it over. Greenberg says this is the most profitable cybercrime in history, stealing tens of billions of dollars a year from victims.

points.h: Passports are confiscated; to buy your freedom you first buy yourself back
points.body: The source, using the name Red Bull, is a computer engineer with a degree from India who was lured to the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos by a "Southeast Asia IT manager" job. On arrival at the compound his passport was confiscated, and he was told the only way to get it back was to "buy it back" — he owed his boss thousands of dollars, covering the cost of bringing him over plus food and lodging, and could only pay off this "contract" through commissions from scamming. Greenberg stresses this is debt bondage: the compound is not a prison of chains and beatings but is packaged as a corporate sales floor, where the boss sends daily motivational messages saying things like "reach out to the next client like you're going to change their life" and "we are on a mission."

Red Bull and his colleagues were constantly fined: for missing contact quotas, for not maintaining fake accounts well enough, for not clocking in on time. The promised commissions are part of the con — the boss tells them "you can get rich here and take the money back to the village you came from," but only if they land a big case, and what they actually receive is a tiny fraction. Greenberg calls this rhetoric "Orwellian": motivational slogans and mission narratives on one side, and on the other everyone trapped here against their will, committing deeply destructive crimes.

points.h: Video calls run on a dedicated face-swap model
points.body: Red Bull says everyone in the compound was trained to use ChatGPT and the Chinese AI chatbot DeepSeek to come up with new topics, polish their language, never run out of well-phrased lines, even write little motivational poems, and find just the right goodnight. More critical is video: the boss required them to discourage victims from video calls as much as possible and stall with excuses; when stalling failed, the compound had a dedicated room and a model who handled video all day, using face-swap software to change the model's face into the photo originally sent to the victim. Greenberg says this kind of software isn't perfect, but by the time a video call happens the victim wants so badly to believe it's real that they overlook the flaws.

points.h: The next step is fully autonomous AI pig butchering
points.body: Greenberg's judgment is that AI is currently just a tool for human scammers, but the next step — already starting to appear — is fully autonomous AI fraud. He cites a case from an Anthropic report the previous week: a Chinese group built 20 dating apps populated entirely by AI, where victims had to keep paying to continue the conversation, and "most" of the other side were fully autonomous large models. He also mentions a study showing that across most of the scam workflow, AI is better than a real person at building relationships — more responsive, more invested, more attentive — which is exactly what the con is doing for the vast majority of the time before it reaches the endgame of asking for money.

points.h: Thirty people, three months, only $2.2 million
points.body: Greenberg gives a concrete scale: Red Bull's group of about 30 people earned only about $2.2 million in total over the three months Red Bull documented and leaked to Wired. This shows pig butchering is a game of probability — a single group's output is limited, but Laos alone has dozens of such compounds, and Cambodia and Myanmar have more, and together they add up to the billions of dollars a year. Greenberg also notes that Red Bull himself was a "very inefficient scammer," which is why he was penniless, eating rice from the compound canteen and vegetables that tasted of strange chemicals, constantly sick, and disgusted by what he was doing.

points.h: Forging a police letter to escape, then beaten when it was seen through
points.body: Red Bull's escape attempt was to forge a letter from the police in his home region of India, saying he was under investigation and had to return to deal with it or his boss would also be in trouble. Greenberg advised him not to do it, but he went ahead, and the forgery was immediately seen through. The boss locked him in a room, beat him, kicked him, withheld food, interrogated him, and even gave him a glass of water with white powder dissolved in it and forced him to drink — Greenberg guesses some kind of stimulant, to make him talk more, while his skin broke out in hives. They never found out he was in contact with a journalist; Greenberg says if they had, he would certainly have been killed.

points.h: The compound moved, and he used it to export all the secrets
points.body: The turning point came when the compound was forced to relocate: the boss seemed to have received word that police in the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos were about to raid it (which later turned out to be more of a performative raid that shut nothing down). The office was first moved into the dormitory, and everyone worked crammed together in the crowded dorm. Red Bull seized the opportunity to send more secrets from his work phone to his personal phone, and at the same time told the boss: you're already struggling to get things done right now, I'm clearly just a burden, let me go and I won't be in your way. To Greenberg's surprise, the boss agreed, essentially throwing him out.

points.h: He chose to come forward with his real name and real face
points.body: Red Bull later revealed his real name to Greenberg: Muhammad Muzahir. Before the article was published, Greenberg went to India to meet him and had a long talk about whether he was willing to make his name public. He decided very clearly that he wanted to, and also appeared in a video Wired produced, because he wanted to inspire people to fight these criminal organizations and stand up for themselves as he had. Greenberg says it was his choice, and of course it carries risks, risks that still trouble him to this day, but he thinks it was an extremely brave thing to do, and that Muzahir is one of the most remarkable sources he has ever worked with.
